blocks.text: A flying weapon to arouse fear, a cloudy arrow (shot) by an unseen archer, a lance at the ready, a spear that moves of itself, a dense phalanx, a sword of a thousand battle-lines, a shifting bulwark of unstable combat. For it does not stand still, but strikes as it runs, lays waste as it creeps, and makes tumult as it flies. It seems to flee, and at once, running back, it stays. 2. They are compared with an army by reason of the order which they keep in flight and on the march. For they are like a strong people set in array for battle (in Hebrew ערוך, drawn up in order). Each will advance in his own ways, and they will not break their ranks, and one will not press upon another. Each will go in his own path. That this is so, Jerome asserts in these words: They fly in such order, by the disposition of God who commands them, that, like the little tesserae which are set in pavements by the hand of the craftsman, they keep their place and do not deviate toward another by so much as a point, so to speak, or a nail's breadth. Nor does he report this from uncertain tradition, but as an eyewitness, αὐτόπτης [autoptēs]. We saw this recently, he says, in this province (of Palestine). And Theodoret: Ἔστι γὰρ ἰδεῖν τὴν ἀκρίδα, τῶν πολεμίων δίκην, καὶ τειχῶν ἐπιβαίνουσαν, καὶ τοῖς ὁδοῖς βαδίζουσαν· καὶ οὐδ᾽ ὑπό τινος ἀνάγκης σκεδασθῆναι ἀνεχομένην, ἀλλ᾽ οἷον μετά τινος συμπνοίας ταύτην ἔφοδον ποιουμένην· [Esti gar idein tēn akrida, tōn polemiōn dikēn, kai teichōn epibainousan, kai tois hodois badizousan; kai oud᾽ hypo tinos anankēs skedasthēnai anechomenēn, all᾽ hoion meta tinos sympnoias tautēn ephodon poioumenēn;] For one may see locusts climb walls like enemies, and advance along the roads; and they do not suffer themselves to be torn apart by any force, but make their [III, 312] attack as if by a kind of mutual conspiracy. And Cyril: Φασὶ δὲ αὐτὰς στοιχηδὸν ἰέναι, καὶ ὡς ἐν τάξει διΐπτασθαι, καὶ ἥκιστα μὲν ἀπονοσφίζεσθαι, περιέπειν δὲ οὕτως ἀλλήλας, ὡσανεὶ καὶ ἀδελφαὶ, φύσεως αὐτῆς [Phasi de autas stoichēdon ienai, kai hōs en taxei diiptasthai, kai hēkista men aponosphizesthai, periepein de houtōs allēlas, hōsanei kai adelphai, physeōs autēs] (read αὐταῖς [autais]) βραβευούσης τὸ φιλάλληλον [brabeuousēs to philallēlon]. They say that they go in order, and fly as if in battle-lines, and are very little separated, and follow one another like sisters, nature dispensing mutual love to them. We have already shown above ^{c)} that the Arabs too, in Damir, teach the same. They gather, they say, كالعسكر [ka-l-ʿaskar] like an army. For when the first of them migrates, all follow and migrate together. And when the first halts, all the rest halt. But most relevant here is that from the Arabic verb نظم [naẓama] nadama, which means to join in a fixed series and to string together, as pearls in a necklace, a swarm of locusts is called منظوم [manẓūm] mandoum. Alcamus: المنظوم الجماعة من الجراد [al-manẓūm al-jamāʿa min al-jarād] Almandoum, a swarm of locusts. Accordingly Sigebert, on the multitude of locusts which ravaged Gaul in the year 874: What is wonderful to tell, it flew in such order, with leaders sent ahead to mark out the camp the day before, that military discipline could be seen in these animals. 3. Like soldiers the locusts scale the walls, [col. 478] march through the city, run upon the wall, climb up into the houses, enter through the windows]. As Moses ^{d)} says to Pharaoh concerning the Egyptian locusts: They shall fill your houses, and the houses of all your servants, and the houses of all the Egyptians. Hence Jerome on Joel: Nothing is impassable to locusts, since they penetrate fields, crops, trees, cities, houses, and the privacy of bedchambers. And Cyril: Οἴκοις αὐτοῖς καὶ πόλεσιν εἰσπεφοιτηκότα, καὶ παρενοχλοῦντα δεινῶς, τὸν ἐκ τῶν ἀκρίδων ἕξουσι στρατόν· [Oikois autois kai polesin eispephoitēkota, kai parenochlounta deinōs, ton ek tōn akridōn hexousi straton;] They will endure an army of locusts that enters their very houses and cities and troubles them dreadfully. Lest this seem incredible, here is an eyewitness beyond all objection, Theodoret, I mean, on this passage! Οὐκ ἀπόχρη τῶν περιβόλων τὸ ὕψος ἐμποδὼν τῇ τούτων εἰσόδῳ γενέσθαι. Ἀλλὰ ῥαδίως μὲν ὑπερβήσονται τὰ τείχη· κλέπταις δὲ παραπλησίως διὰ θυρίδων εἰς τὰς οἰκίας εἰσελεύσονται. Καὶ τοῦτο δὲ οὐ μόνον ὑπὸ πολεμίων, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑπὸ ἀκρίδων γεγενημένων [Ouk apochrē tōn peribolōn to hypsos empodōn tē toutōn eisodō genesthai. Alla rhadiōs men hyperbēsontai ta teichē; kleptais de paraplēsiōs dia thyridōn eis tas oikias eiseleusontai. Kai touto de ou monon hypo polemiōn, alla kai hypo akridōn gegenēmenōn] (read γεγενήμενον [gegenēmenon]) πολλάκις ἐθεασάμεθα. οὐ πετόμεναι γὰρ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ κατὰ τῶν τειχῶν ἀνερποῦσαι, διὰ τῶν φωταγώγων εἰς τοὺς οἴκους εἰσίασι. [pollakis etheasametha. ou petomenai gar monon, alla kai kata tōn teichōn anerpousai, dia tōn phōtagōgōn eis tous oikous eisiasi.] The height of the walls is not enough to prevent their (the enemies') entry. For they will easily climb over the walls, and, like thieves, will enter the houses through the windows. This we have often seen done not only by enemies but also by locusts. For not only by flying, but also by creeping up the walls, they penetrate into houses through the windows. And Pliny had already noted that locusts also come to houses and gnaw everything with their bite, even the doors of buildings. So Hieronymus Mercurialis [III, 313] gives as a sign of the plague of Venice and Padua that many bruchi had appeared along the streets and walls. And so in the histories of the Arabs I find that locusts sometimes fall onto their tables. Thus in Tabrani, Algesen, son of Ali, says: We were sitting at table and feasting, I and my brother Muhammed, son of Alchanaphia, and the sons of my paternal uncle, Abdalla, and Kethem, and Alphadal, sons of Alibas, فوقعت الجرادة على المايدة [fa-waqaʿat al-jarāda ʿalā al-māyida] and a locust fell upon the table, etc. Damir collected more of this kind, from which it is plain that they penetrate into the houses of the Arabs. 4. They rush through missiles (or through swords) and are not wounded.] For other animals flee at the sight of a man, but these attack a man of their own accord. Accordingly, when a cloud of locusts comes on, everyone hides in the houses, lest by going out they provoke them. Democritus in the Geoponica, book 13: Ἐὰν νέφος ἀκρίδων ἐπέρχηται, πάντες ἔνδον μενέτωσαν ἀφανεῖς, καὶ παρελεύσονται τὸ χωρίον [Ean nephos akridōn eperchētai, pantes endon menetōsan aphaneis, kai pareleusontai to chōrion]. Nor is there reason to hope that they can be driven off by brandished weapons. For they are carried along with a blind rush, and neither fear swords nor are easily wounded by them. By their lightness, namely, and the slenderness of their little bodies, they elude any blows. Moreover, as Claudian rightly observed,
